item.content:encoded:
Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026.
El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempos recientes.
Treinta y ocho expertos de MLB.com emitieron sus votos sobre quiénes creen que se llevarán los honores de JMV tras esta temporada, con 32 jugadores recibiendo al menos un voto. Como recordatorio, los votos se basaron no solo en el desempeño hasta ahora, sino también en cómo se espera que evolucionen las cosas durante el resto de la campaña.
Los votantes clasificaron a sus cinco principales candidatos de cada liga con un sistema de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por el segundo, y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
Todas las estadísticas son hasta la jornada del domingo, a menos que se indique lo contrario.
LIGA AMERICANA
Álvarez ha tenido un desempeño tan bueno este año que lo que califica como un bache para él sería un gran trecho para la mayoría de los demás bateadores. En sus últimos 41 encuentros, batea .264 con OPS de .840. Reiteramos, nada mal para la mayoría, pero muy por debajo del nivel del líder de la Americana en promedio (.313) y OPS (1.027). Álvarez lleva tres cuadrangulares y cinco impulsadas a lo largo de 16 partidos este mes, dejándolo a un jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero de los Rays por el liderato en el Joven Circuito y a seis empujadas de Pete Alonso por la cima en dicho departamento. Aunque sus posibilidades de la Triple Corona se están desvaneciendo un poco, Álvarez todavía ha armado un 2026 asombroso en el plato. Su wRC+ de 179 es al menos 27 puntos mejor que el de cualquier otro bateador calificado.
Sabemos que el quisqueyano es uno de los grandes cañoneros del juego. Está cerrando su segunda temporada consecutiva de 40 vuelacercas y está dando swings más fuerte que nadie. Pero lo que ha sido más impresionante de su temporada es su mejorado criterio en la zona de strike. Aumentó su tasa de boletos desde un 6.3% por debajo del promedio a un 11.5%, lo que se ubica en el 80mo percentil de MLB. También ha mantenido una tasa de ponches muy sólida (18.5%). Ya no persigue tantos pitcheos fuera de la zona, ha reducido su tasa de swings en blanco y está haciendo más contacto en general. Esa mezcla de paciencia, trueno y control del bate es una combinación especial, sobre todo en un jugador de 23 años. Luciendo un porcentaje de embasarse de .363 (52 puntos mejor que la campaña pasada), el OPS de .892 de Caminero se ubica tercero en la Americana.
Witt ha tenido mejores campañas a la ofensiva, aunque 18 bambinazos, 43 estafadas y wRC+ de 119 en 137 partidos no está nada mal. Pero cuando se consideran todas sus capacidades, Witt sigue siendo extremadamente valioso. Su valor de carreras defensivas de +16 está empatado en el tercer lugar de las Grandes Ligas, y sus 22 outs por encima del promedio encabezan la Liga Americana. También cuenta con un valor de carreras en el corrido de bases de +8, a uno de Corbin Carroll de los Diamondbacks por el liderato de MLB. Por eso, aunque no ha sido tan indiscutible en la caja de bateo como lo fue en el 2024 (wRC+ de 169), la grandeza integral de Witt lo tiene en la cima de la tabla de posiciones de WAR de FanGraphs en el Joven Circuito (6.6) y posiblemente perfilándolo entre los primeros cinco en la votación para JMV por tercera vez en tres años.
Ha habido bastante conversación de JMV entorno a Schlittler en las últimas semanas. ¿Y por qué no? Está marcando el paso en la Americana en efectividad (1.94), WHIP (0.91) y WAR de pitcheo de FanGraphs (6.1). Se ubica segundo en el Joven Circuito en promedio de bateo en contra (.182) y en tasa de ponches menos boletos (25.0%). Ha permitido una carrera o ninguna en 21 aperturas. Ese es un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees y algo que apenas otros dos lanzadores de 25 años o menos han logrado en la Era de la Pelota Viva (desde 1920): Blake Snell (2018) y Dean Chance (1964). Seguramente será reconocido con el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana a estas alturas, pero Schlittler recibirá su merecida cuota de consideración para el JMV.
Schlittler no ha sido el único miembro de los Bombarderos que ha sido indispensable este año. Mientras Nueva York ha estado sin Aaron Judge durante una gran parte de la campaña y ha echado de menos a otros bates estelares debido a lesiones, Rice ha sido demostrado consistencia. Se ubica tercero en el Joven Circuito en jonrones (39) y anotadas (100). Es cuarto en la liga en impulsadas (95) y OPS (.888), y está empatado en el cuarto lugar en valor de carreras al bate (+34). Con dos vuelacercas durante la última semana, Rice se convertiría en apenas el segundo miembro del equipo del Bronx diferente a Judge en la última década en conectar al menos 41 jonrones en una temporada, acompañando al dominicano Juan Soto (2024).
Otros que recibieron votos: El venezolano Willson Contreras, Medias Rojas; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigres; el cubano Miguel Vargas, Medias Blancas; el cubano Randy Arozarena, Marineros; Munetaka Murakami, Medias Blancas; Dylan Cease, Azulejos.
LIGA NACIONAL
El mes pasado, PCA dio el salto por encima de Ohtani hacia el puesto Nro. 1 de nuestra encuesta. Este mes, se ha apartado por completo del resto del grupo. Crow-Armstrong, quien recibió cada voto de primer lugar emitido por nuestro panel, está empatado con Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de bambinazos de MLB (45). Nadie tiene más anotadas (118), extrabases (83) o total de bases anotadas (351) esta campaña. Con 38 estafadas, el dinámico jardinero central del equipo del Norte de Chicago podría convertirse en el séptimo miembro del club 40-40 más adelante esta semana. Y no pase por alto el hecho de que es posiblemente el mejor jugador a la defensa en cualquier posición en estos momentos. Ya no es una cuestión de si Crow-Armstrong es el JMV de la Nacional. El premio es prácticamente suyo ahora mismo. Pero ¿lo ganará de manera unánime?
Ohtani se mantiene como el claro escolta en el Viejo Circuito a pesar de haber jugado en apenas tres partidos este mes debido a sus persistentes lesiones en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho. La buena noticia es que el dirigente de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, dijo que "hay una buena posibilidad" de que Ohtani sea activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días el miércoles tras cumplir la estadía mínima. No lanzará por el resto de la temporada, dejándolo con efectividad de 1.79 y 95 ponches en 85.2 entradas. Pero Ohtani tendrá unos cuantos partidos para sumar a sus totales ofensivos (30 jonrones, wRC+ de 142).
Mencionamos antes cómo Schlittler luce como el gran favorito para el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Misiorowski tendría su premio más asegurado en la Nacional. A lo largo de 169.1 episodios, Miz encabeza la Gran Carpa en casi cada categoría, incluyendo efectividad (1.86), WHIP (0.80), tasa de ponches menos boletos (31.7%) y fWAR (6.5), por nombrar solo algunas. Sus oponentes tienen un diminuto OPS de .474 contra Misiorowski, la segunda menor cifra para cualquier abridor calificado en la Era Divisional (desde 1969). Los oponentes del quisqueyano Pedro Martínez, en una de las mejores campañas para un lanzador, registraron OPS de .473 en el 2000.
El dominicano, quien no recibió un solo voto en nuestra anterior encuesta de JMV, ha estado encendido con Cincinnati durante el último mes. En sus últimos 27 encuentros, batea .404 con ocho vuelacercas, seis bases robadas y OPS de 1.205. Dio múltiples hits en 14 de esos partidos, y su fWAR de 2.5 durante este transcurso es el mejor de las Mayores. Esta prolongada racha encendida le ha dado a De la Cruz un wRC+ de 139 -- el mejor de su carrera -- y lo deja a dos jonrones más dos estafadas de convertirse en el cuarto jugador de los Rojos en el club 30-30 y el primero desde Brandon Phillips en el 2007.
Schwarber ha caído en un pequeño bache, bateando de 34-4 con un cuadrangular en sus últimos 10 encuentros. También está a ocho ponches de establecer un récord de ponches en una misma campaña. De todas maneras, hay que admirar la consistencia de Schwarber. Terminará con más de 40 vuelacercas y 150 juegos disputados en cuatro de las últimas cinco temporadas. Ha superado los 100 boletos negociados por cuarto año consecutivo, y un tercer título de bambinazos del Viejo Circuito está a su alcance.
Otros que recibieron votos: El dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Cerveceros; Matt Olson, Bravos; James Wood, Nacionales; Jordan Walker, Cardenales; Alex Bregman, Cachorros; Bryce Harper, Filis; Jake Bauers, Cerveceros; el dominicano Otto López, Marlins; el venezolano Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Rafael Devers, Gigantes; Alec Burleson, Cardenales; CJ Abrams, Nacionales; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez, Filis.

item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

item.content:encoded:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
Some baseball dreams begin with the finest equipment, elite coaching and scouts waiting to spot the next big star. José Ramírez's journey began very differently. The Cleveland Guardians star grew up with limited resources, faced doubts about his potential and had to fight for recognition. Years later, he reached 1,000 career RBIs, turning an overlooked beginning into a remarkable MLB story.
José Ramírez's humble beginnings in the Dominican Republic
Long before thousands of fans cheered his name at Progressive Field, Ramírez was a young boy in Baní, a city in the Dominican Republic, trying to make the most of whatever baseball equipment he could find.
His family faced financial struggles, and even getting a proper glove was difficult. In a 2023 MLB feature, Ramírez recalled the challenges his family faced while he was growing up.
“It was difficult for my dad,” he said through interpreter Agustin Rivero. “He didn’t have much work, we didn’t have much money. I had to play with a glove that was too tight.”
That small detail offers a glimpse into the reality of Ramírez's early life. For him, baseball was never simply a game played for fun. It represented a chance to change his family's circumstances and build a future beyond the financial limits he knew as a child.
Before he began playing organised baseball, Ramírez and other neighbourhood children played Vitilla, a popular Dominican street game. They used plastic water jug caps as balls and sticks as bats. The makeshift equipment could not match what elite prospects used, but the children made the most of what they had.
Ramírez also faced a challenge that had nothing to do with money. His small frame made him easy to overlook in a sport where scouts often search for size, strength and physical potential.
Yet, the young infielder kept showing up and competing. His story was taking shape long before a Major League Baseball team gave him a chance.
MLB scouts overlooked José Ramírez despite his talent
Ramírez's road to professional baseball was anything but straightforward. While other young players attracted attention at showcases in the Dominican Republic, he often found himself waiting on the sidelines.
By the time he was 17, his chances of securing a professional contract appeared to be slipping away. Many of the top Dominican prospects signed with MLB teams at 16, leaving Ramírez behind as scouts focused on younger players with more conventional physical profiles.
He was frequently used as a fill-in at showcases rather than receiving the same opportunities as the headline prospects. His lack of size and limited scouting attention made it harder for him to stand out, even when his performance suggested he deserved a closer look.
Ramírez later described the doubts he faced in an ESPN interview, recalling how people judged him before he had the chance to prove himself.
“I knew it would be hard for me [to get signed] because [scouts] are always looking for a Mike Trout, a Bryce Harper. Those kind of guys; big, strong guys. I imagine that [José] Altuve had the same thing happen to him. I guess nobody believed Altuve could be what he has become. Sometimes your size, a smaller body, one does not attract attention or anything and nobody believes in you,” he said.
The lack of interest could have ended his dream before it truly began. Instead, Ramírez continued to play, trusting his ability even when the people evaluating him did not share that confidence.
His opportunity finally arrived in 2009. During a showcase, Cleveland's scouting director John Mirabelli and scout Ramón Peña watched him play second base. Ramírez delivered three hits that day, followed by three more the next day and five hits during a doubleheader.
Peña pushed for Cleveland to sign him. The Guardians' organisation, then known as the Indians, eventually offered Ramírez a $50,000 signing bonus.
It was a modest investment compared with the money given to highly sought-after international prospects. But that decision would become one of the most significant signings in the franchise's history.
José Ramírez turned a modest signing into an MLB career
Even after signing with Cleveland, Ramírez had no guarantee of becoming a major league star. His small signing bonus did not bring the same expectations or opportunities that came with a lucrative prospect contract.
He had to earn his place at every level, moving through the Dominican Summer League, the Arizona Rookie League and several other Minor League stops. There were no shortcuts. Each promotion required him to prove that his performance could translate against stronger competition.
Cleveland's front office later acknowledged that Ramírez did not arrive with the attention usually reserved for elite prospects. His progress came through steady work rather than early hype.
That gradual rise makes his career particularly striking. Ramírez developed into one of baseball's most consistent hitters, combining contact skills, speed, power and versatility. He also became a switch-hitter capable of putting pressure on opposing pitchers from either side of the plate.
His success challenged the assumptions that had limited his opportunities as a teenager. The traits that once made him easy to overlook did not prevent him from becoming a central figure in Cleveland's lineup.
Over time, Ramírez became far more than a promising player who exceeded expectations. He established himself as a franchise cornerstone, a perennial offensive threat and a player whose contributions extended well beyond individual statistics.
The journey also reflects the importance of the people who believed in him early. Peña continued to advocate for Ramírez when others saw little reason to invest in him. That faith gave the young Dominican infielder an opening, but Ramírez still had to turn it into a career.
José Ramírez reaches 1,000 career RBIs with the Guardians
On September 18, 2026, Ramírez added another defining moment to his career. The Guardians star crushed a solo home run against the Athletics at Progressive Field, recording his 1,000th career RBI during Cleveland's 5-3 victory.
The milestone came in the sixth inning, with his 401-foot blast giving the home crowd another reason to celebrate a player who had spent years earning their admiration.
Ramírez became just the second player in Cleveland franchise history to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Earl Averill. He also became the 12th active MLB player to reach the mark.
For a player who once struggled to attract the attention of scouts, the achievement carries a special meaning. It reflects years of consistency, development and the ability to deliver when his team needs him.
Guardians manager Stephen Vogt captured the scale of the accomplishment by putting it in perspective.
“I like to use those round numbers,” Vogt said. “[It’s] 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done, right?”
Ramírez, however, remained focused on the team's success rather than his personal achievement.
“Thank God for the opportunity to play here for this organization and be able to achieve [1,000 RBIs],” Ramírez said through team interpreter Agustin Rivero. “But most important is that we're able to win today, because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
That mindset helps explain why Ramírez's story resonates beyond the milestone itself. His journey is about more than proving scouts wrong. It is about turning a difficult start into a career built on persistence, consistency and loyalty to the game.
From a young boy playing with an ill-fitting glove in Baní to one of Cleveland's most accomplished hitters, José Ramírez has shown that a player's beginning does not have to define his ceiling. His 1,000th RBI is another chapter in a story that is still being written.
Reporting note: The career milestone and game details are based on MLB's September 19, 2026, report. The early-life details are drawn from MLB's 2023 profile and ESPN's reporting on Ramírez's rise.

As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez.
Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight game remaining.
In that win, Ramirez went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs, which gave him 1,000 RBIs in his career. In doing so, he became the 12th active player to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Mike Trout, Bryce Harper, Nolan Arenado, Andrew McCutchen, Salvador Perez, Eugenio Suarez and Carlos Santana.
“Very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and to be bale to achieve that,” Ramirez said through a team translator. “But the most important part is that we’re able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
Jose Ramirez stats
He’s also just the second Cleveland player to hit that milestone with the franchise, joining Earl Averill (1,084), whose playing career ended in the early 1940s.
It’s a significant line on Ramirez's Hall of Fame resume. The home run also brought him within three of becoming only the ninth player in MLB history to reach the 300/300 club for home runs and stolen bases.
“I like to use round numbers,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “It’s 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it’s incredible what he has accomplished, and he’s not even close to being done. And very few people get do it, and it’s really cool to be here to watch it.”
It was a milestone night for Ramirez, though it came at the end of what has been one of his more frustrating seasons, particularly over the last few weeks while he’s played through hamate been surgery rehab.
Jose Ramirez injury update
He’s posted a 90 wRC+, which would be the first time since he became a full-time player in 2016 he’s been below 100 (league average). Since he returned to the lineup on July 22, after the procedure, he’s hit .216 with a .567 OPS.
“I keep working on it every day,” Ramirez said. “I have to keep working in the training room every day because this type of injury is the type where one day you feel good, the next you don’t feel so well, but you have to keep grinding.”
Despite the lack of his usual MVP-caliber production on a nightly basis, Vogt and the Guardians have still applauded the way Ramirez has fought through the situation. It’s one of the attributes that often gets mentioned first when listing why they feel he’s so valuable to the organization.
“Even as he was coming back and we have to give him off days, he was not happy about it,” Vogt said. “He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day. We know that there’s days where he’s not feeling good and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day.
“It’s such a great example for our young guys to see that just because you’re not feeling 100 percent, it doesn’t mean you can’t go out and compete and contribute to help the team win.”
Ryan Lewis covers the Guardians for the Beacon Journal. He can be reached at rlewis1@gannett.com.

CLEVELAND -- As the Progressive Field crowd roared around him, José Ramírez paused and leaned back in the left-handed batter’s box to admire his work. There was no doubt where the baseball he launched to right field was headed.
That image has played on repeat over the past 14 seasons. This time, it came with a heavy dose of history, and it was well-timed as the Guardians continue to push for the postseason.
Ramírez tallied his 1,000th career RBI on Friday by launching his 297th career home run, in the sixth inning of the Guardians’ matchup with the A’s in the opener of a three-game series. The superstar third baseman joined Earl Averill (1,084) as the only players in Cleveland franchise history to hit the RBI milestone.
The Guardians improved to 79-75 with their third straight win. They entered Friday with the same record as the White Sox, but Chicago technically led the division because it holds the tiebreaker over Cleveland after winning the season series.
It means the Guardians must finish with more wins than the Sox to win the Central for a third straight year. Ramírez helped; his towering blast went a Statcast-projected 401 feet and had a 102.4 mph exit velocity.
Ramírez, who turned 34 years old on Thursday, is now just the 12th active player with 1,000 career RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Nolan Arenado, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Andrew McCutchen, Carlos Santana, Bryce Harper, Salvador Perez, Mike Trout and Eugenio Suárez.
The home run was Ramírez’s first since Aug. 30 and just his 12th this season. He entered Friday with an uncharacteristic .683 OPS in 117 games, in an injury-impacted campaign after he missed five weeks following left hamate surgery.
Ramírez has been dealt with the effects of that procedure since he came off the injured list on July 22. On Friday, he reminded us he’s always just one swing away from impacting a game in a big way.

The Mets (70-84) defeated the Philadelphia Phillies (85-69) by a score of 6-3.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Mets left-handed starter Zac Thornton plunked leadoff batter Kyle Schwarber on a 3-2 count to get the game started. The rookie battled back, striking out Trea Turner and Bryce Harper before Mets first baseman Brett Baty made a diving stop on a Luis Arraez grounder down the line to put away the third out.
-- Southpaw Tim Mayza served as the bullpen opener for Philadelphia, and Francisco Lindor jumped all over him with a leadoff double. With one out, Bo Bichette worked a 10-pitch at-bat, culminating in a single to center field which moved Lindor up to third base. Carson Benge kept the line moving and drove in Lindor with an opposite-field single. Mark Vientos was walked to load the bases, and Phillies manager Don Mattingly pulled Mayza for right-handed reliever Jose Urquidy. A.J. Ewing roped an Urquidy fastball for a double, which scored two runs. Urquidy retired the next two Mets batters to limit the damage to three runs.
-- In the second inning, Ewing got turned around on a deep line drive to center, failing to haul in the RBI double for Bryson Stott, which cut the Mets' lead to 3-1. In the bottom half of the inning, Juan Soto doubled into the left-center field gap with two outs, but Urquidy struck out Bichette to end the threat.
-- With two outs away in the top of the sixth, Phillies left fielder Edmundo Sosa blasted a solo shot to left field, his third hit of the night. Excluding Sosa, Thornton allowed just two hits. He struck out four and walked one, allowing two earned runs across 87 pitches.
-- Soto took a hanging breaking ball thrown by Phillies right-hander Orion Kerkering 428 feet for a two-out three-run homer in the bottom of the sixth. Soto's 26th tater of 2026 put the Mets up 6-2.
-- Philadelphia center fielder Derek Hill responded with a solo home run off of Mets left-handed reliever Nate Lavender in the top of the seventh. Lavender persevered, retiring each of the next four batters he faced, before handing the ball to Dedniel Núñez to record the third out of the eighth. In the bottom half of the frame, Bichette grounded into a double play with the bases loaded. Núñez handled the ninth inning and retired the side to earn the first save of his season - and second save of his career - to seal the 6-3 win for the Mets.
Game MVP: Juan Soto
Soto notched his third game with multiple extra-base hits in September, going 3-for-5 with a double and a three-run homer. It was also Soto's third game of the season with at least three hits.

Yordan Alvarez has been the American League's best hitter in 2026. But is that enough for him to be crowned AL MVP? The Astros' designated hitter has one week left to hold off young Rays superstar Junior Caminero, who has made a surge for the award in recent weeks.
There's no denying that the Astros' slugger has had a monster season, hitting .311 with 40 homers and 99 RBI in 149 games entering Friday. He currently leads the AL in on-base percentage (.429), slugging (.598) and OPS (1.027). And he has stayed healthy and played in all but four of Houston's games, allowing him to put together a remarkable season.
When it comes to winning MVP, the numbers are critically important, and the narrative of the season plays a part as well. But an often overlooked aspect of award voting, particularly for MVP, is historical precedent.
Alvarez is a primary designated hitter, and prior to Shohei Ohtani's historic 50/50 season in 2024, in which he did not pitch but won NL MVP, no primary DH had ever won the MVP Award. Ohtani in 2024 is still the only DH to do it, given that in his other MVP seasons, he also pitched.
Considering his singular status as a two-way player, Ohtani is the exception to this rule. Besides him, no full-time designated hitter has ever won MVP. In fact, since 2000, only six designated hitters have finished in the top five of MVP voting. That list includes Frank Thomas (second in 2000, fourth in 2006), David Ortiz (fifth in 2003, fourth in 2004, second in 2005, third in 2006, fourth in 2007), Travis Hafner (fifth in 2005), J.D. Martinez (fourth in 2018), Marcell Ozuna (fourth in 2024) and Kyle Schwarber (second in 2025). Alvarez finished third in 2022 while splitting time between DH and outfield.
Among designated hitters since 1995, here are five of the top seasons comparable to Alvarez's 2026 and where they finished in MVP balloting:
- Edgar Martinez, 1995: .356/.479/.628, 182 H, 29 HR, 113 RBI, 182 wRC+, 7.0 fWAR — third
- Frank Thomas, 2000: .328/.436/.625, 191 H, 43 HR, 143 RBI, 160 wRC+, 5.9 fWAR — second
- David Ortiz, 2005: .300/.397/.604, 180 H, 47 HR, 148 RBI, 157 wRC+, 5.3 fWAR — second
- David Ortiz, 2007: .332/.445/.621, 182 H, 35 HR, 117 RBI, 175 wRC+, 6.3 fWAR — fourth
- J.D. Martinez, 2018: .330/.402/.629, 188 H, 43 HR, 130 RBI, 170 wRC+, 5.8 fWAR — fourth
- Yordan Alvarez, 2026: 311/.429/.598, 166 H, 40 HR, 99 RBI, 177 wRC+, 6.2 fWAR — ?
When you look at what Alvarez has accomplished this season, his numbers with eight games to play are right in line with those of his elite DH contemporaries. But if designated hitters who put up similar seasons weren't able to win MVP, will the Astros' slugger be able to reverse that trend?
Short of playing a defensive position, Alvarez has done everything he can to hold off Caminero, but the Rays' third baseman has made a push over the past month. The 23-year-old, who has earned the title of best player on the AL's best team, is slashing .277/.363/.532 with 41 home runs and 96 RBI this season. Although he rates out poorly defensively, Caminero has appeared in 151 games and counting at the hot corner. Plus, he delivered his potential MVP moment with a walk-off homer to clinch a playoff berth for the Rays.
One of the things working against Alvarez is the fact that, after being on pace to do so for most of the season, he is now unlikely to win the AL Triple Crown. Entering Friday, he's tied with Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson for the league lead in batting average, he's second to Caminero in home runs, and he's second in RBI behind Baltimore's Pete Alonso.
Recent history tells us that a historic season, like Ohtani's 50/50 season in 2024 or Aaron Judge's AL-record 61 home runs in 2022, can provide the narrative juice to pave the way to MVP, making the Triple Crown Alvarez's best path to the award this year. Only Miguel Cabrera in 2012 has accomplished that feat in the past 60 years. Without the Triple Crown, it'll likely be tougher for Alvarez to sway voters.
Another thing that's likely hurting Alvarez's case is how poorly the Astros have played in 2026. They might be one of the worst division winners in MLB history, or they could still miss the postseason completely. That said, there's precedent for this in recent MVP voting, as Bryce Harper won the 2021 NL MVP Award on an 82-80 Phillies team that missed the postseason.
Over the past six seasons, the AL MVP Award has been dominated by Ohtani and Judge, with very little argument in the years they've won. But this season, with Alvarez and Caminero, voters will be selecting a new winner, and they'll have to decide what's most important in determining most valuable.
For the Astros' slugger, we'll wait to see if a nearly historic season by a designated hitter can be enough.

item.content:encoded:
Many fans rely on numbers to tell the story of a baseball season. For 2026, I’m going with letters. Here’s the story of the regular season from A to Z.

A: Yordan Alvarez: He’s the only qualifier in baseball with an OBP of over .400. He’s leading the American League in batting, on-base, slugging, OPS, and walks. Where would Joe Espada’s Astros be without him? Yordan is still the favorite to win the American League MVP, despite his numbers falling off a bit down the stretch.
B: Bryan Baker: Tampa Bay scored 698 runs and allowed 618 in games through September 17. That would give them a record of 84-68 according to the Pythagorean Theorem. But they were 93-59, nine games better. Credit in part goes to their closer Baker, leading the league with 40 saves this season..
C: Pete Crow-Armstrong: When the Cubs suffered through a 10-game losing streak in May, Pete batted just .161 (5-36 AB) in those 10 games. In games through September 17, PCA in 85 Cubs victories: .357/.442/.740. He scored 89 runs in 85 Cubs wins. The NL MVP by a mile. You cannot tell the story of the 2026 season without talking about Pete Crow-Armstrong.
D: Jacob deGrom: On September 10, deGrom started against the Mariners in Seattle. In six innings, he faced just 19 batters, one over the minimum. He struck out 12, gave up one hit, walked none, and didn’t allow a run. He left the game with Texas leading by three runs. The bullpen flushed away the lead and Texas wound up losing the game. The story of deGrom’s career. Jacob is historically significant. He has started 277 games in his career, and three of his top 10 (ranked by Pitchers’ Game Score) have come in 2026.
E: Errors: There’s only been one season EVER with fewer errors per game than 2026. Of course, that would be 2025. No pitcher has made more than four errors this season. In 1969, Jim Kaat won a Gold Glove, despite making eight errors (tied for the MLB lead with Boston’s Ray Culp among pitchers). Gold Gloves were all reputation in those days. In fact, Kaat’s longtime Minnesota teammate, Zoilo Versalles, won a Gold Glove in 1965 despite making 39 errors!
F: Freddie Freeman: Freeman has hit 32 doubles this year and 579 in his career. Is 579 doubles a lot? Well, that’s 90 more than the next-closest active player, Paul Goldschmidt. And when Freddie legs out his 600th, he’ll become only the 19th player with at least 600 doubles. He’s a little more than a season away from passing both Hank Aaron (624) and Barry Bonds (601).
G: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.: Vlad Jr. hit a home run every 25 at-bats in 2025. He’s hit a home run every 58 at-bats in 2026. He didn’t hit his first home run at home this year until Toronto’s 75th home game. He had gone 84 straight home games without a homer.
H: Bryce Harper: In March, Harper hit a two-run game-tying homer in the 8th inning of the WBC Finals. This season, his wRC+ (139) has been one of the top dozen in the majors. In October, can he lead the Phillies to his first World Series championship?
I: Raisel Iglesias: The Braves have spent all season in first place, and Iglesias is a big part of that. In the last 10 years (2017-2026) only one player (Kenley Jansen) has more saves than Iglesias. He’s 33-for-36 in save chances this year for the Braves. But here’s the thing: over the last five years, he’s saved 130 games for the Braves, but only one in the postseason. That has to change.
J: Aaron Judge: #99 missed 99 days (84 games) this season with a rib injury, but the three-time MVP came back in mid-September with enough time to get his timing back at the plate. Yankees fans will have to hope that the leg tightness isn’t a big deal.
K: Steven Kwan: There hasn’t been a hotter hitter in the American League since the start of July. Kwan is batting .350 since July 1, and .351 since the All-Star break. The Guardians have needed every bit of his offense, as José Ramírez has not been the same since returning from his broken left hamate bone.
L: Brandon Lowe: In his first season with Pittsburgh, Lowe has hit a career best 30 homers and has an OPS over .800. The Pirates offense was one of the big stories of the first half of the 2026 season, and Lowe was a big reason why. In the second half, injuries to Oneil Cruz and Ryan O’Hearn have sunk the Bucs but the offense was fun while it lasted.
M: Jacob Misiorowski: Milwaukee has the best record in baseball, and he’s a big reason why. Has any Brewers pitcher ever had a better season than the 24-year-old ace? Sorry, fans of Teddy Higuera. The answer is no. “The Miz” leads the majors in strikeouts (243). He leads the majors in ERA (1.89). He’s striking out more than 13 batters per nine innings! Misiorowski has had 1,053 pitches this season over 100.0 mph. No one else in pitch tracking era (2008-present) has had a season of 1,000 or more.
N: No-Hitters: On May 25, three Astros pitchers Tatsuya Imai (6 IP), Steven Okert (1 IP), and Alimber Santa (2 IP) combined to complete the Astros’ fifth combined no-hitter in franchise history. No one pitcher has completed a no-hitter since Blake Snell did it in August of 2024 for the Giants.
O: Shohei Ohtani: There are two players whose last name starts with “O” with more homers than Ohtani this season: Matt Olson and Kazuma Okamoto. But Ohtani made 14 brilliant starts (1.79 ERA) and his wRC+ of 142 is in the top 10 in the game.
P: Salvador Perez: The 36-year-old put up nearly 600 at-bats this season. And while most of them came as a DH or 1B, he did start 44 games behind the plate. In his 15-year career, he’s caught 1,427 games (1,396 starts) and nearly 12,000 innings.
Q: Quick games: On September 7, in an afternoon game at Citizens Bank Park, the Phillies beat the Braves 1-0 in a game that took 1:51 to play. On June 16 at Dodger Stadium, the Dodgers defeated the Rays 1-0 in a game that took 1:52 to complete. And in early April, the Royals defeated the White Sox in games on April 10 and 11 that lasted in 1:54 and 1:55, respectively. Thank you, pitch clock.
R: Eduardo Rodriguez: The Diamondbacks have won 22 of E-Rod’s first 30 starts. Talk about valuable! He has a 2.62 ERA this season (it was 5.04 and 5.02 in the two previous seasons). This is his best year since 2019.
S: Cam Schlittler: Is he the AL MVP, or just the AL Cy Young? The Yankees won 20 of his 31 starts. The Yankees don’t need a lot of offense when he takes the mound. He has a 1.14 ERA in 16 road starts this season! Since earned runs became official in both leagues in 1913, Schlittler’s 1.14 road ERA is the fourth best (minimum 15 road starts). The top three: Bob Gibson in 1968 (0.81 ERA); Walter Johnson in 1913 (1.06 ERA); and Greg Maddux in 1995 (1.12 ERA).
T: Bruce Turang: What a player! His OPS has gone up in each of his first four seasons. He’s now a 20 HR/20 SB/100 runs/100 RBI player. The Brewers need him to improve his performance in last year’s NLCS vs. the Dodgers, when he went 1-for-15 (.067).
U: Uncle Charlie (curveball): The curveball is heading toward extinction, much like individual no-hitters. Curveballs have only accounted for 6.4% of pitches this season, the second lowest rate since first tracked in 2008 (2024: 6.1%). That’s pure curves, not including slow curves or knuckle-curves. Want to know which pitcher has thrown the most curveballs (including knuckle and slow curves) this year? Philadelphia’s Aaron Nola, at 942.
V: Miguel Vargas: The White Sox have been one of the best stories this year, and we could have given the “V” to manager Max Venable. But Vargas’ 31 home runs and stealing 19 bases in 21 attempts makes him the choice. Vargas has a 4.7 WAR this season, up from 1.9 last year.
W: Willson and Wilyer, the heart of the Boston lineup. Right fielder Wilyer Abreu leads the American League with 36 doubles. He also leads the AL in outfield assists with 12. Willson Contreras has an OPS of .905, second in AL to Alvarez, even ahead of Rays slugger Junior Caminero. Remember, Boston was 14 games under .500 as late as June 24. And then the season turned around.
X: Xander Bogaerts: The Padres have played well down the stretch and now appear likely to reach the postseason. And X-Man has contributed, stealing 21 bases in 22 attempts this year. It’s no fluke, either. He stole 20 of 22 last season. In his four seasons with the Padres, he has stolen 73 bases in 81 attempts. That’s efficiency.
Y: Yoshinobu Yamamoto: The Dodgers’ Yoshinobu Yamamoto has a 1.98 ERA in 10 starts after the All-Star break. He’s probably the key to the Dodgers’ chances of completing a three-peat. Who can forget what he did last October, when he went 5-1, with a 1.45 ERA in 37.1 postseason innings.
Z: Zack Wheeler: From July 21 through August 24, Wheeler had a stretch of seven starts that saw him give up 26 runs (25 earned) in 31.1 innings (7.18 ERA). He was terrific in the first half and recaptured his form down the stretch. If the Phillies are going to go deep into October, they’ll need Wheeler (and their other two aces) to be at the top of their game.
Editors’ Note: Elliott Kalb - dubbed “Mr. Stats” decades ago by Marv Albert and Bob Costas - is the former Senior Editorial Director at MLB Network and a longtime contributor of research and information to NBC Sports’ telecasts.
